catalog_quote: In Kristang most polysyllablic words fall into two large classes according to the position of stress in the word. These classes follow two stress rules: Stress Rule A. Most words which end in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable, as in kaza (= ka + za) 'house' ... kumeria (= ku + me + ri + a) 'food' ... Stress Rule B. Most words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable, as in landes (= lan + des) 'Dutch', natal (= na + tal) 'Christmas'. Nevertheless, stress is not completely predictable in Kristang as there are certain words which are exceptions to the above two rules. Exceptions to rule A (i) One large class of exceptions to rule A above consists of verbs which end in a stressed vowel. [fn.24: However, some disyllabic verbs, such as podi 'to be able', are normally stressed on the penultimate syllable.] Here, the dictionary follows the practice of Bahasa Mela…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are verbatim in the held at Introduction section 5 pp. xiii-xiv (fn.23-24) and section 7 pp. xiv-xv, as the locator says. (2) The deciding source is a dictionary introduction, but it is by the language's reference grammarian and restates his grammar (Baxter 1988 section 2.6 = Baxter 1984 thesis section 2.6 pp.63-69, held in full and read here): penult for V-final non-verbs, final for C-final words, verbs final with lexical exceptions, plus clause-level verb stress retraction — i.e. the record's Rule A/B + verb exception + word-domain hedge is exactly Baxter's analysis, and the 'weight-hedged, CVC, right edge, non-strict' coding matches. sources.quote: 'MPC differs from Malay as it has lexical stress' (p.93). 'the stressed syllable is longer and has a higher intensity compared to the unstressed ones ... In general, MPC has a large number of words displaying penultimate syllable stress, as in kaza [ˈka.zə] house, floris [ˈflo.ris] flower. This is especially the case in words ending in a vowel, provided they are not verbs. A second large class of words, principally verbs, take final-syllable stress, for example, kumí [ku.ˈmi] ... However, even in cases where we may predict word-final stress ... the speaker sometimes stresses the first syllable
sources.note: Only IPA Illustration / quasi-instrumental statement on Kristang stress; confirms the V-final-penult / C-final-final / verbs-final picture and documents verb-stress variability in running speech; worth adding to refs as the modern corroborating source.
